Thank you for making this video. I really needed to hear this. Reading so many comments about how kids who put their sick or dying parents in nursing facilities are heartless and selfish, was really starting to get to me. Especially when I know how much I loved my mom.

Me and my mom had a very close relationship. I loved my mom so much 😢. A year ago she was diagnosed with pancreatic and ovarian cancer. Within months, her health declined horrifically. Me, my dad and 2 siblings all assisted with taking care of her. It was the most terrifying, traumatic and helpless experience I’ve ever endured.. My mom was no longer able to move her body and loss the ability to swallow or control muscles in her throat. She would constantly vomit dark blood, and because she could no longer control any muscles in her body, she would choke on her own vomit. That freaked me out so much!

It was at that point my mom said she wanted to go to a hospice facility, because she required too much medical attention, and she didn’t want to feel like a burden on us. My exact words to my mom was “Ma…,you know how much I love you, right? (She nodded her head). I love you so much, Ma. But this is too much for me. I can’t do all this. I don’t feel like I can give you the type of care you need.” It was a mutual understanding. My mom knew how much I loved her.

Thank you so much for this video! I cannot say that I'm in the exact shoes of some of the middle-age caregivers you are describing, but I can relate somewhat. I'm almost 55 and my mother is almost 91 and she has dementia. She lives in a group home a mile away from me, and I moved her in there last summer. So although I don't do the feeding, bathing, diaper changing, I still take her to all of her medical appointments on my own. It's impactful enough where I can only manage a part-time job. A full-time job would not be possible.

I am grateful that she has long-term care insurance so we can have her in that home and the insurance pays for it all. I would think that it would be impossible for me to have any kind of life whatsoever if I had to personally take care of her.

You are not kidding about the guilt! I feel so much guilt about having moved her into a group home, because she is bored, lonely, depressed, and miserable there and she never lets me forget it, every time I visit her. But she is so cognitively compromised that she cannot empathize at all with why I had to make this decision.

snippet.textDisplay: We have been taking care of my mother in law for 9.75 years.  She is now 98.  It's gradually gotten more difficult and now after a hip fracture in May we are helping with diaper changes, cleaning up accidents, helping her dress, picking her up off the floor and doing more than we've ever had to do.  We always said that as soon as we started dealing with diapers we would be done, but now that the time is here the other family members (who never volunteer to help by the way) are indicating they don't want to see Mom in a nursing  home.  We are thankful to have found a good caregiver, trained by hospice, who assists with baths for a couple of hours 3 times per week and watches her while we go on one outing together once per week to attend church.  I wish she would have had such a conversation with us as you've described in telling us at what level to put her into a home and relieved the guilt....but she isn't that kind of person - she has said "she never will go to a nursing home and not to put her there". We know she would be angry and never forgive us.  We are trying to hang on a little longer and praying she will peacefully pass away at home; however her organs are good, her mind is good and we could be in this for a few more years.  It's very difficult and we see no way out, which is making for a very depressing and frustrating situation.

snippet.textDisplay: For the last 4 and a half years, I had an adversarial relationship with my mother who I loved, but I hated the elderly person she had become.  She was having ever increasing problems related to her mobility and intestinal problems, and she refused to move out of her home and into an independent living facility.  2 months ago she had a severe stroke.  After she spent a night in the hospital, we were able to get her transported to a hospice facility where she died 2 days later.  My mom NEVER wanted to have that discussion with me or my sister as to how to plan elder care or end of life care for her, which in my opinion was incredibly shortsighted and selfish of her.  Although I miss my mother, I’m so glad she went as quickly as she did.  So many people in my situation aren’t as fortunate and have to endure the stress of fighting and arguing with elderly parents under far worse circumstances than I did.

snippet.textDisplay: Thanks, for the most honest picture of care giving I've heard, in a long time. The government policy, where I live, is to download care, to the families, without any concern, for the physical, psychological and financial burden. Even if you have a POA, good luck putting them in a nursing home or even accessing crappy "at home" services, if the patient can still utter the word "no." I am caring for my mother, with Alzheimer's.  She came to the disease, with a bevy of serious, untreated mental illness.  It's impossible to describe how combative, abusive, stubborn and reckless she is.  I honestly wish I was dead. I will NEVER do this, to my children.  In my living will, it states clearly, that if I'm cognitively impaired, my family is empowered to place me in residential care, notwithstanding any objections, from my demented self. I have also stipulated that, if I can't manage my own food, I am not to be spoon or tube feed.  You have to write this stuff down, when you're competent.  Once you have dementia, you probably won't recognize your own deficits.

snippet.textDisplay: I did a study on the history of nursing homes. If the family didn't take care of their aging loved ones they either died on the side of the road or were put into institutions where they usually died lying on a dirty cot. Nursing homes today are only good for one thing. Taking the person's property away from them and all their social security and retirement while they smoke cigarrettes outside. I should know, because my wife told me about all the horror stories of the places she worked as a CNA. Don't stick mom or dad in a home unless it means you'd have to go homeless yourself. The bare minimum a child should do for their agaging parent is to visit frequently. Not once a month or just on holidays like some do. It's not an option.

snippet.textDisplay: In my view, the main problem is that people choose to get their children increasingly at older ages for various reasons. They even propagate "social freezing". This is a totally selfish attitude because the consequence is that these people require care taking exactly then when their children are in the process of developing their careers or are on top of their career. I went through this and it totally destroyed my career as a scientist. And this is true even if you have the resources to put your parents in an elderly home since you loose you geographic mobility that is required to develop your career. My advice: get your kids while you are young. This is the best proof of love to your kids. Hardly anybody is talking about this extremely important aspect.

snippet.textDisplay: You are completely correct. But what is the solution?? I came back to my home town 2 states away to help care for my 92 year old dad who had a stroke. He saved money and had funds for his care. It severely impacted my health, job and wellbeing to have to manage everything. He died at 94 after a not great hospice journey. The hospice aides were great. Our hospice nurse was burnt out. I hired caregivers and supervised it all. Now I have my 91 year old mother at home with caregivers half the day. Our caregivers are great and I very much appreciate them. This being stuck caregiving old parents sucks.  My life on hold. My dad was my nurturing parent. My mother was all about looks and hated that she couldn’t live the life she wanted. She parentified me and dumped her problems on a 6, 8 10 year old me. I tried my whole life to make them happy.  If you’ve had some happy loving supportive family, count your blessings. Don’t judge and be supportive. Many of us have not.  I think there should be a number to call to place elders in NH for 7-10 days. Pay privately or charity. There should be an unquestionable relief for adult children stuck in this.

RN who's worked long-term care, hospice and now, ICU. We are completely unrealistic about the societal shift that has taken place. We no longer have women in the homes as caregivers for a population that's now living longer than ever!

Not to mention many of us are heavier than ever, which doubles the physical burden of care!

I will do as much as I can for my parents, but I would not wish a caregiving life on my kids in their - and my - old age.
